name: Folic acid
className: Folic acid and derivatives (B group vitamin)

src.q: Each tablet contains 5.0mg Folic Acid

bnf.note: BNF/BNFC is only available in the UK; not accessed.

items.t: Folate-deficient megaloblastic anaemia (malnutrition, malabsorption, increased need as in pregnancy). Not to be used alone in undiagnosed megaloblastic anaemia, pernicious anaemia or macrocytic anaemia of unknown cause unless given with enough hydroxocobalamin.

src.q: For the treatment of folate-deficient megaloblastic anaemia due to malnutrition, malabsorption syndromes (such as coeliac disease or sprue) and increased utilisation as in pregnancy.

It should not be used alone in undiagnosed megaloblastic anaemia including in infancy, pernicious anaemia or macrocytic anaemia of unknown aetiology, unless administered with adequate amounts of hydroxocobalamin.

items.t: Prophylaxis of drug-induced folate deficiency (e.g. phenytoin, phenobarbital, primidone); prophylaxis in chronic haemolytic states or renal dialysis.

src.q: For the prophylaxis of drug induced folate deficiency e.g. caused by administration of phenytoin, phenobarbital and primidone.
For the prophylaxis against folate deficiency in chronic haemolytic states or in renal dialysis.

items.t: Prevention of neural tube defects in women planning pregnancy who are known to be at risk.

src.q: For the prevention of neural tube defects for woman planning a pregnancy and known to be at risk.

items.t: The 5 mg tablet is not intended for healthy pregnant women (lower doses are recommended); it is for folate deficiency or women at risk of neural tube defect recurrence.

src.q: This product is not intended for healthy pregnant women where lower doses are recommended, but for pregnant women with folic acid deficiency or women at risk for the reoccurrence of neural tube defect.

items.t: Adults: 5 mg daily for 4 months; up to 15 mg daily may be needed in malabsorption.

src.q: In folate deficient megaloblastic anaemia : 5mg daily for 4 months; up to 15mg daily may be necessary for malabsorption states.

items.t: Adults: 5 mg daily for 4 months; up to 15 mg daily in malabsorption.

src.q: In drug induced folate deficiency : 5mg daily for 4 months; up to 15mg daily may be necessary for malabsorption states.

items.t: 5 mg every 1-7 days depending on the underlying disease.

src.q: For prophylaxis in chronic haemolytic states or in renal dialysis : 5mg every 1- 7 days depending on underlying disease.

items.tag: Prevention of neural tube defects (women at risk)
items.t: 5 mg daily, started before conception and continued through the first trimester.

src.q: Prevention of neural tube defects in women known to be at risk : 5mg daily started before conception and continued throughout the first trimester.

items.t: 5 mg daily continued to term.

src.q: Pregnancy: In established folate deficiency: 5mg daily continued to term.

items.t: SPS: folic acid 5 mg once weekly on a different day from methotrexate is the most commonly recommended regimen to reduce methotrexate adverse effects (off-label use).

src.q: Folic acid 5mg weekly, on a different day to the methotrexate dose, is the most commonly recommended regimen from clinical studies and national guidance.
Use of folic acid to reduce adverse effects is off-label.

items.t: Child 1-18 years: 5 mg daily for 4 months; maintenance 5 mg every 1-7 days. For young children use a more suitable dosage form.

src.q: In folate deficient megaloblastic anaemia: Child 1-18 years 5mg daily for 4 months; maintenance 5mg every 1-7 days.
For young children a more suitable dosage form should be used.

items.t: Child 1-12 years: 2.5-5 mg once daily. Child 12-18 years: 5-10 mg once daily.

src.q: In haemolytic anaemia; metabolic disorders: Child 1-12 years 2.5mg-5mg once daily. Child 12-18 years 5-10mg once daily.

items.t: Child 1-12 years: 250 micrograms/kg (max 10 mg) once daily. Child 12-18 years: 5-10 mg once daily.

src.q: Prophylaxis of folate deficiency in renal dialysis: Child 1-12 years 250 microgram/kg (max 10mg) once daily. Children 12-18 years 5-10mg once daily.

items.t: Long-term folate in untreated cobalamin (vitamin B12) deficiency, including untreated pernicious anaemia and lifelong vegetarians: it can precipitate cobalamin neuropathy and subacute combined degeneration of the cord. Never give folic acid alone for Addisonian pernicious anaemia or other B12 deficiency.

src.q: Long-term folate therapy is contraindicated in any patient with untreated cobalamin deficiency.

Folic acid should never be given alone in the treatment of Addisonian pernicious anaemia and other vitamin B12 deficiency states because it may precipitate the onset of subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord.

items.t: Malignant disease, unless megaloblastic anaemia due to folate deficiency is an important complication.

src.q: Folic acid should not be used in malignant disease unless megaloblastic anaemia owing to folate deficiency is an important complication.

items.t: Hypersensitivity to folic acid or any excipient.

src.q: Known hypersensitivity to folic acid or any of the excipients listed in section 6.1.

items.t: Vitamin B12 deficiency must not be treated with folic acid unless enough hydroxocobalamin is also given: folic acid can mask it while nerve damage continues.

src.q: Patients with vitamin B12 deficiency should not be treated with folic acid unless administered with adequate amounts of hydroxocobalamin, as it can mask the condition but the subacute irreversible damage to the nervous system will continue.

items.t: Caution in patients who may have folate-dependent tumours.

src.q: Caution should be exercised when administering folic acid to patients who may have folate dependent tumours.

items.t: Contains lactose and sucrose: not for people with hereditary galactose intolerance, total lactase deficiency, glucose-galactose malabsorption, fructose intolerance or sucrase-isomaltase insufficiency.

src.q: Patients with rare hereditary problems of galactose intolerance, total lactase deficiency or glucose-galactose malabsorption should not take this medicine.
Patients with rare hereditary problems of fructose intolerance, glucose-galactose malabsorption or sucrase-isomaltase insufficiency should not take this medicine.

items.t: Correcting folate deficiency lowers plasma phenytoin, with possible loss of seizure control. A similar but weaker effect occurs with other anticonvulsants, including carbamazepine, valproate and barbiturates.

src.q: Correction of the folate deficiency reduces plasma phenytoin with potential loss of seizure control.
Similar but less marked relationship exist with all anti-convulsant treatments including sodium valproate, carbamazepine and the barbiturates

items.t: Folic acid may interfere with the toxic and therapeutic effects of methotrexate. Folate deficiency caused by methotrexate or trimethoprim cannot be treated with folic acid: use folinic acid. SPS: folic acid is routinely given with methotrexate in rheumatoid arthritis to reduce adverse effects, usually not on the methotrexate day.

src.q: Folic acid may interfere with the toxic and therapeutic effects of methotrexate.
Methotrexate and trimethoprim are specific anti-folates and the folate deficiency caused by their prolonged use cannot be treated by Folic Acid Tablets BP. Folinic acid should be used.
Folic acid supplements are usually avoided on the day of oral or subcutaneous methotrexate.

items.t: Co-trimoxazole and chloramphenicol may interfere with folate metabolism.

src.q: Antibacterials - chloramphenicol and co-trimoxazole, may interfere with folate metabolism.

items.t: Sulfasalazine and triamterene inhibit folate absorption. Folate enhances lithium efficacy. Nitrous oxide may cause acute folate deficiency. Ethanol and aspirin increase folate elimination.

src.q: Sulphasalazine and triamterene also inhibit absorption.
Folate supplements enhance the efficacy of lithium therapy.
Both ethanol and aspirin increase folic elimination.

items.t: No renal dose adjustment stated. Used for folate prophylaxis in renal dialysis (5 mg every 1-7 days). Folic acid is removed by haemodialysis.

src.q: For prophylaxis in chronic haemolytic states or in renal dialysis : 5mg every 1- 7 days depending on underlying disease.
Folic acid is removed by haemodialysis.

hepatic.note: No hepatic impairment advice in the UK folic acid 5 mg tablet SmPC.

items.t: No known hazards in pregnancy; folic acid supplements are often beneficial. Folate deficiency is linked to neural tube and other birth defects.

src.q: There are no known hazards to the use of folic acid in pregnancy, supplements of folic acid are often beneficial.

items.t: BUMPS: most women need about 400 micrograms daily before conception and for the first 12 weeks; a higher 5 mg dose is prescribed for some (e.g. some medicines such as for epilepsy, diabetes, or a family history of neural tube defect).

src.q: Most women are advised to take a supplement containing a daily dose of around 400 micrograms (mcg) of folic acid.

If you are taking certain medicines (for example, to treat epilepsy), have a health condition like diabetes, or have a close family member with a neural tube defect, your doctor will prescribe you a higher daily dose of 5 milligrams (mg) folic acid.

items.t: Folic acid passes into breast milk; no adverse effects seen in breastfed infants.

src.q: No adverse effects have been observed in breast fed infants whose mothers were receiving folic acid.

items.t: Women planning pregnancy who are at risk of neural tube defects: 5 mg daily from before conception through the first trimester.

src.q: Prevention of neural tube defects in women known to be at risk : 5mg daily started before conception and continued throughout the first trimester.

items.t: No common effects listed. Rare: anorexia, nausea, abdominal distension, flatulence.

src.q: Anorexia, nausea, abdominal distension and flatulence

items.t: Rare allergic reactions, including anaphylaxis (shock).

src.q: Allergic reactions, comprising erythema, rash, pruritus, urticaria, dyspnoea and Anaphylactic reaction (including shock)

items.t: In untreated B12 deficiency, folate for 3 months or longer has precipitated cobalamin neuropathy.

src.q: Folate given to such patients for 3 months or longer has precipitated cobalamin neuropathy.

items.t: Exclude untreated vitamin B12 deficiency before long-term folate. In elderly people do a cobalamin absorption test before long-term therapy.

src.q: In elderly people, a cobalamin absorption test should be done before long-term folate therapy.

items.t: For oral use.

src.q: Method of administration For oral administration.

items.t: If taken with weekly methotrexate, take folic acid on a different day from the methotrexate (SPS).

src.q: Folic acid supplements are usually avoided on the day of oral or subcutaneous methotrexate.
Known hypersensitivity to folic acid or any of the excipients listed in section 6.1.

rules.action: Long-term folate is contraindicated; never give folic acid alone - give with adequate hydroxocobalamin. The SmPC says short courses of folate do no harm.

No harm results from short courses of folate.

src.q: Folic acid should not be used in malignant disease unless megaloblastic anaemia owing to folate deficiency is an important complication.
